steps.label: KP09 Architecture and training drive the revival
The revival timeline · 1/10
steps.speakerNotes: 1980, 1986, 1989, 1998, 2006, 2012 and 2017 are selected papers, each tied to a different question: local representation, multilayer learning, data and compute, sequence architecture.

steps.label: The revival timeline · 1/10 (1)
steps.speakerNotes: LeNet-5 in 1998 and layer-wise pretraining in 2006.

steps.label: The revival timeline · 1/10 (2)
steps.speakerNotes: AlexNet in 2012 and the Transformer in 2017. The timeline marks different feasible conditions and methods.

steps.label: The revival timeline · 1/10 (3)
steps.speakerNotes: No single algorithm woke deep learning: data representation, trainability, compute and the task objective together change what is feasible.

steps.label: Locality and weight sharing · 2/10
steps.speakerNotes: Neighboring image pixels usually form local patterns. This page uses a 4-by-4 single-channel input, a supplementary example.

steps.label: Locality and weight sharing · 2/10 (1)
steps.speakerNotes: A 2-by-2 filter slides over the input with stride 1 and no padding, over 9 positions.

steps.label: Locality and weight sharing · 2/10 (2)
steps.speakerNotes: Every position uses the same 4 weights, called weight sharing; with local connectivity, a new position needs no new parameters.

steps.label: Locality and weight sharing · 2/10 (3)
steps.speakerNotes: The output is translation-equivariant; do not call it fully translation-invariant.

steps.label: Parameters of one layer · 3/10
steps.speakerNotes: A supplementary controlled example: a 4-by-4 single-channel input, 2-by-2 kernels, stride 1, no padding, two 3-by-3 output maps, 3 times 3 times 2 equal to 18 outputs.

steps.label: Parameters of one layer · 3/10 (1)
steps.speakerNotes: If each output connects to all 16 pixels with its own bias: 16 times 18 plus 18, which is 306 parameters.

steps.label: Parameters of one layer · 3/10 (2)
steps.speakerNotes: If two convolution kernels are reused at every position: 2 times (2 times 2 plus 1) equals 10 parameters. Bars are drawn to 306 and 10. This compares one layer with the same output shape and does not mean a CNN is smaller or more accurate overall.

steps.label: Parameters of one layer · 3/10 (3)
steps.speakerNotes: Both counts were computed and checked by program.

steps.label: Three different milestones · 4/10
steps.speakerNotes: Fukushima's 1980 Neocognitron used hierarchy, local receptive fields and reuse of similar features to handle position changes; it is not the later LeNet-5 trained end to end by backpropagation.

steps.label: Three different milestones · 4/10 (1)
steps.speakerNotes: LeCun et al.'s 1989 ZIP-code recognition showed an early trainable convolutional network.

steps.label: Three different milestones · 4/10 (2)
steps.speakerNotes: The 1998 paper “Gradient-Based Learning Applied to Document Recognition” describes the specific architecture LeNet-5. So “LeNet 1989” and “LeNet-5 1998” are not the same model or paper.

steps.label: Three different milestones · 4/10 (3)
steps.speakerNotes: This is where the note corrects a confusion in the source.

steps.label: From trainable to scalable · 5/10
steps.speakerNotes: The 1986 back-propagation milestone did not make every deep network easy to train at once. With depth, gradient flow, initialization, data scale and hardware became obstacles, while kernel methods and SVMs stayed valuable in some settings.

steps.label: From trainable to scalable · 5/10 (1)
steps.speakerNotes: In 2006 there are two separate Hinton-related papers: Hinton, Osindero and Teh's Deep Belief Nets proposed greedy layer-wise learning; Hinton and Salakhutdinov studied deep autoencoders for dimensionality reduction. The source mixes the authors; both belong to the revival, but are not one paper.

steps.label: From trainable to scalable · 5/10 (2)
steps.speakerNotes: In 2012 Krizhevsky, Sutskever and Hinton's AlexNet broke through on ImageNet by combining large labeled data, GPUs, ReLU, data augmentation and dropout.

steps.label: From trainable to scalable · 5/10 (3)
steps.speakerNotes: Describing the 1990s to 2006 as total hibernation hides continuing work on CNNs, speech and recurrent networks.

steps.label: Sequences and attention · 6/10
steps.speakerNotes: RNNs and LSTMs process sequences with a recurrent state passed along step by step.

steps.label: Sequences and attention · 6/10 (1)
steps.speakerNotes: Attention can pick information across positions, but the 2014 to 2015 encoder-decoders with attention could still contain RNNs, so attention had not yet removed recurrence.

steps.label: Sequences and attention · 6/10 (2)
steps.speakerNotes: The 2017 Transformer paper explicitly replaced recurrence with attention in its sequence-transduction architecture, improving training parallelism.

steps.label: Sequences and attention · 6/10 (3)
steps.speakerNotes: In 2018 BERT represents encoder-style pretraining and GPT the autoregressive generation route. Different architectures serve different input and output needs. The figure is a sketch.

steps.label: Generative models · 7/10
steps.speakerNotes: Generative models answer how to produce data-like samples. VAEs use latent variables and a variational objective; Kingma and Welling's preprint is 2013 and the conference version 2014.

steps.label: Generative models · 7/10 (1)
steps.speakerNotes: GANs use an adversarial generator and discriminator, 2014.

steps.label: Generative models · 7/10 (2)
steps.speakerNotes: Diffusion models learn step-by-step reverse generation. Sohl-Dickstein et al.'s diffusion paper is from 2015; Ho et al.'s 2020 DDPM was an important improvement, not the first appearance.

steps.label: Generative models · 7/10 (3)
steps.speakerNotes: Sample quality, coverage, training and sampling cost depend on implementation and data; no class can be claimed better across the board. The figures are sketches.

steps.label: Preference alignment · 8/10
steps.speakerNotes: Preference alignment is a different problem. Typical RLHF first estimates a preference reward model, then optimizes the policy. Do not claim every RLHF uses the same steps.

steps.label: Preference alignment · 8/10 (1)
steps.speakerNotes: The 2023 DPO paper gives a direct preference-optimization objective that avoids a separately fitted explicit reward model, but still depends on preference data and reference-policy conditions.

steps.label: Preference alignment · 8/10 (2)
steps.speakerNotes: Do not turn “no extra reward model” into “no human preferences”.

steps.label: Preference alignment · 8/10 (3)
steps.speakerNotes: The note's 4 self-check questions stay in the note.

steps.label: Data structure and methods · 9/10
steps.speakerNotes: Images, sequences, graphs, generation and preferences are different entry points. Images suggest CNNs; sequences suggest RNNs, LSTMs and Transformers.

steps.label: Data structure and methods · 9/10 (1)
steps.speakerNotes: Graphs have ChebNet, GCN and GAT; generation has VAEs, GANs and diffusion models.

steps.label: Data structure and methods · 9/10 (2)
steps.speakerNotes: Human preferences point to RLHF and DPO. Misconception: CNN, Transformer, GNN, generative models and DPO are not versions replacing each other; some are input structures, some architectures, some objectives or procedures. Ask the question first, then compare conditions.

steps.label: Data structure and methods · 9/10 (3)
steps.speakerNotes: The arrows point to method candidates and do not claim a one-to-one rule.

steps.label: Limits and next step · 10/10
steps.speakerNotes: Deep RL: DQN approximates action values with a network, while AlphaGo also uses tree search and cannot be equated with a single DQN. Few-shot and self-supervised: signals from the data itself do not mean no objective.

steps.label: Limits and next step · 10/10 (1)
steps.speakerNotes: Graph data: GCN's preprint and conference years differ. Deployment and risk: federated learning does not guarantee privacy and compression can change quality, so measure each separately.

steps.label: Limits and next step · 10/10 (2)
steps.speakerNotes: Rule of thumb: start from data structure and objective, then weigh architecture, training and cost. The next unit turns the chapter's tasks, methods and history into a decision map.

steps.label: Limits and next step · 10/10 (3)
steps.speakerNotes: The note's 4 self-check questions stay in the note.
